method_card.title: Histograms and Frequency Density
method_card.content:
A histogram with unequal class widths uses frequency density on the y-axis. This is a Higher-tier only skill.

Important: the formula \(\text{frequency density} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}\) is NOT given on the formula sheet — you must recall it.

The reason for using frequency density is that the area of each bar represents the frequency, not the height. If frequency were plotted on the y-axis with unequal class widths, wider classes would appear taller even with the same number of items, misleading the reader.

The two core directions to master:

  • Forward (frequency → density): calculate the class width, then divide the frequency by the class width.
  • Reverse (density → frequency): multiply the bar height by the class width to recover the frequency. This is the more commonly tested direction.

To find the total frequency, sum all recovered frequencies (each = height × class width). Recognising misrepresentation: if someone draws a histogram with unequal class widths but plots frequency on the y-axis, wider bars are misleadingly tall. This is a listed misrepresentation error.
steps: Recall the formula: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width (not on formula sheet)
Calculate each class width from the interval boundaries
Forward: divide frequency by class width to get bar height
Reverse: multiply bar height by class width to get frequency
Sum all recovered frequencies to find the total
Check by confirming total area = total frequency

exam_context.marks: 3–6 marks; forward and reverse calculations are typically 1 mark each; full problems combining both directions are 4–6 marks
exam_context.frequency: Appears on most Higher tier papers; the reverse calculation (density × width = frequency) is tested more often than the forward direction

worked_examples.question: A class interval 20–30 has frequency 15. Calculate the frequency density for this bar.
A histogram bar for class 40–60 has frequency density 3.5. What is the frequency for this class?
A histogram shows four bars: Class 0–10: height 2.4; Class 10–20: height 3.8; Class 20–40: height 1.9; Class 40–70: height 0.6. Find the total frequency.

bronze.display: A class interval 0–5 has frequency 20. What is the frequency density?

misconceptions.message: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Do not use frequency as the bar height.

bronze.display: A class interval 10–30 has frequency 40. What is the frequency density?
A histogram bar for class 5–15 has height (frequency density) = 3. What is the frequency?

misconceptions.message: Frequency = frequency density × class width = 3 × 10 = 30. The bar height is NOT the frequency.

bronze.display: A histogram bar for class 20–50 has frequency density 1.6. What is the frequency?
Which formula correctly gives the frequency density for a histogram bar?
options: Frequency × class width
Frequency ÷ class width
Class width ÷ frequency
Frequency + class width

misconceptions.message: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. This formula is NOT on the formula sheet.

bronze.display: Class 0–20 has frequency 36. Class 20–30 has frequency 24. Which class has the greater frequency density?
options: Class 0–20 (width 20)
Class 20–30 (width 10)
Both have the same frequency density
Cannot tell without the histogram

misconceptions.message: Class 0–20: density = 36/20 = 1.8. Class 20–30: density = 24/10 = 2.4. Class 20–30 has the greater density despite fewer items.

bronze.display: A bar for class 0–4 has frequency density 5. What is the frequency?
A histogram bar for class 100–200 has height 0.8 (frequency density). What is the frequency?

silver.display: A frequency table: class 0–10: 25; 10–20: 40; 20–40: 30; 40–80: 20. Calculate the frequency density for class 20–40.
A histogram: class 0–10 has height 4.5, class 10–30 has height 2.2. What is the combined frequency?
Class 0–5 has frequency density 6; class 5–15 has frequency density 3. What is the total frequency across both classes?
Class 0–20 has frequency density 2.5; class 20–25 has frequency density 8. Which class has the greater frequency?
options: Class 0–20 (frequency 50)
Class 20–25 (frequency 40)
Both classes have the same frequency
Class 20–25 (frequency 8)

misconceptions.message: Class 0–20: 2.5×20=50. Class 20–25: 8×5=40. Class 0–20 has greater frequency despite its lower bar height.

silver.display: A frequency table: class 0–10: 35; 10–20: 35; 20–50: 42. What is the frequency density for class 20–50?
A histogram: Class A (0–5) height 3.2; Class B (5–10) height 4.0; Class C (10–20) height 1.8. What percentage of the total is in Class B?

gold.display: A histogram: Class 0–10: fd=1.8; Class 10–25: fd=3.2; Class 25–40: fd=2.4; Class 40–60: fd=0.9. What is the total frequency?
Classes 10–20 and 20–30 have frequency densities 4.5 and 3.5 respectively. A student claims both represent the same frequency. Are they correct?
options: Yes — both bars have equal class widths so frequency = density for both
No — class 10–20 has frequency 45 and class 20–30 has frequency 35
Yes — the same class width means the same frequency
No — you need more information to determine the frequencies

misconceptions.message: Both widths = 10. 10–20: 4.5×10=45. 20–30: 3.5×10=35. Different densities, same width → different frequencies.

gold.display: A histogram: Class 0–10: height 2.0; Class 10–20: height 5.0; Class 20–50: height 1.0. Estimate the number of values in the range 15–30.

misconceptions.message: 15–20 (half of class 10–20, width 5): 5.0×5=25. 20–30 (one-third of class 20–50, width 10): 1.0×10=10. Total ≈ 25+10=35. Note: assumes uniform distribution within classes.

gold.display: Class 0–20 has frequency density 3.5. The frequency in class 20–30 is twice the frequency in class 0–20. Find the frequency density h of the class 20–30 bar.

misconceptions.message: Class 0–20 frequency = 3.5×20=70. Class 20–30 frequency = 2×70=140. Class width=10. h = 140÷10 = 14.

gold.display: A histogram is drawn with unequal class widths but with frequency (not frequency density) on the y-axis. Classes 10–20 and 20–40 both have frequency 30. The bars appear equally tall. Explain the misrepresentation.
options: No error — equal frequencies produce equal bar heights
The y-axis should show frequency density; the 20–40 bar should be half the height of the 10–20 bar because its class is twice as wide
The 20–40 bar should be twice the height because it covers twice the range
Frequencies should always be on the y-axis for accuracy

misconceptions.message: With unequal widths, using frequency on the y-axis misleads: the 20–40 bar covers twice the range of 10–20 but appears equally tall. Frequency density corrects this: 10–20 density = 30/10 = 3; 20–40 density = 30/20 = 1.5.

gold.display: A histogram: Class 0–10: fd=1.5; Class 10–15: fd=6.0; Class 15–20: fd=4.0; Class 20–40: fd=0.75. What fraction of all values are in class 10–15? Give your answer in simplest form.
